rv.q: In George Bernard Shaw’s “Caesar & Cleopatra,” adapted and directed by David Staller in a briskly entertaining, winningly down-to-earth revival for Gingold Theatrical Group, the young queen of Egypt is charming in her naïveté.
The friction produced is reliably funny and frequently poignant.

What makes Gingold Theatrical Group artistic director David Staller ' s new adaptation of Caesar and Cleopatra so delightful, though, is how deftly he and his splendid cast bring these historical figures and others down to earth, without downplaying the moral questions that inform the work—about authority, vengeance, temperance and love.

Under the astute direction of the Gingold Theatrical Group’s David Staller, Cuccioli, Lim, Braxton and company offer a charming and historic way to spend an evening with a witty and unfamiliar Shaw comedy.
The swiftly moving mounting provides plenty to fascinate and entertain.
This revival is a series of advances and retreats; I'm awfully glad that Shaw has such a defender in Staller, but I hope that in the future he doesn't feel any need to apologize for him.
See Caesar and Cleopatra if you are a Shaw completist — you may not have another opportunity to see this ho-hum historical comedy for a long time.

David Staller’s direction is both evenhanded and refreshing, successfully bring this adaptation to an authentic and innovative staging of this Shaw classic that has not been produced in New York in over forty years.

The Gingold production fails to make the case that Caesar and Cleopatra is a masterpiece, but, working on a puny budget, Staller and his cast have done some sort of justice to this interesting, rarely staged work.
But in the end, Shaw’s play floats, never truly living up to its potential, but not sinking into the deep dark ocean that surrounds them.
If Shaw's Caesar and Cleopatra is a Sphinx's riddle, this halting production hasn't solved it.

cn.t: Shaw's mentor-protégé comedy charms critics in Staller's brisk, entertaining production, with strong leads and clever staging earning praise despite some questioning the director's unconventional choices.
